persons.name: Richard Borum
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Borum, Richard' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). persons.name: Samuel Lewis
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'SAMUEL LEWIS' and 'SAMUEL LEWIs,' and 'SAMYEL LEWIS,' and 'Samuel Lewis' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 12 August 1835, column 5; the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 29; the Democrat of 9 July 1834, column 1; the Democrat of 16 July 1834, column 1; the Democrat of 22 July 1835, column 5; the Democrat of 29 July 1835, column 8, and 1 further mention(s). The corpus associates the name with A. Garrett's Auction Room, South Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `schoolteacher` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Samuel Lewis as a schoolteacher at Chicago 7 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. persons.name: James Panster
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST ALONE. Read from poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Panster, James” (poll_1835_055, line 342). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Panster' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.

citations.citation: The first Chicago Catholic church register — Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's marriage register and his death and burial page — as printed and annotated in the *Illinois Catholic Historical Review*, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922), and republished in two pages by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team. 128 dated marriages of 1834-1839, each naming groom, bride, witnesses and officiating priest, and 11 deaths and burials of June 1834 to March 1837.

transcribes.work: The first Chicago Catholic church record, kept by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from 1833 and continued by Fathers Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara to 1839
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and nobody in this project has seen it. What is read here is a 1921-22 article that prints the marriage entries and the death entries and comments on them. The article itself says the death record 'is contained on a single page' of the book.

transcribes.work: Illinois Catholic Historical Review, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922)
transcribes.note: The layer actually read, at one further remove: the Genealogy Trails team transcribed these two pages out of the Review and this project read the transcription. Every record citing this source is graded transcription_mediated, twice over.

what_it_supplies: 128 marriages at Chicago (125 of them) between 1834 and 1839, each dated, and each naming its witnesses BY NAME — 513 named readings of people standing at a named place on a named day
six marriages IN THE SCENE YEAR, which with their witnesses put twenty named people in Chicago on five days of 1835
eleven deaths and burials, four of them in 1835, including the death of Thomas Owen, agent of the Indians, at Chicago on 15 October 1835
the register's own arithmetic — 22 St. Cyr marriages, 18 Schaeffer, 87 O'Meara, 1 Plunkett — which verifies any reading of it without the book
the dates bounding each priest's time at Chicago, which is what makes an unsigned entry attributable
the Irish, French and German Catholic population of the town, which is the part the poll books and letter lists reach least well
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town
any age, except for three infants and one nine-year-old on the death page
the baptisms. The article tallies 282 of them by these same priests and prints none; that register is T-0503's object and is not in this source
residence. A marriage at Chicago on a day of 1835 is presence on that day, and presence is not residence
reliable spelling. The article says so itself: a French and German priest writing Irish and English names, and an Irish priest writing French and German ones
